p: Friday, May 14, Tributary answered Nate's question in one paragraph. Its disaster recovery plan would get its first full test in January, as part of a new yearly program, and Cascade was welcome to observe. One Chart would go live in October.
Nate called before Maria had finished reading it. So the first time anybody finds out if it works, he said, is three months after three hospitals depend on it.

The design phase had started that week. By the end of July, every decision about how One Chart would run in Wyoming had to be on paper and signed: how it would recover, what its data meant, what moved and what didn't. Corvane's build team would be in Cheyenne in June. Kiran had left at 5:10 every night that week. Maria had checked.
At 9:14 that night, on the couch, her phone buzzed.
A text from Theo Reyes. Had lunch with Irene in Greeley last week. She still asks about you. Every single time. I'm sending you her number so you can't tell me you lost it. Call her.

Maria hadn't lost it. She'd had Irene's number for eighteen years. She'd left Irene's retirement party early in 2022 for a meeting she couldn't remember now, and she'd meant to call the next week, and then it had been four years. Theo had been her partner on nights for ten years. He was the only person who could have sent that text.

She called at 9:31, before she could think of a reason not to. It rang four times. Maria Santos, Irene said, the way she used to read a name off the census board. Theo said you might. Tomorrow at ten. You remember the house. She hung up before Maria could apologize, which was also how she'd run report.
Lucia had heard every word from the other end of the couch. Who's Irene? The woman who got me hired. You sound scared of her. Everybody was, Maria said. That's how you knew she was good.

Saturday, May 15, Irene Kowalski's house was where it had always been, a brick ranch on a corner in west Greeley with a crab apple tree in the front yard. Maria sat in the driveway with the engine off for six minutes by the dashboard clock. Then the front door opened. A woman with short gray hair came down the walk jingling her keys, spotted the car, and changed course.

Well, I'll be, the woman said, and tapped on the glass until Maria rolled it down. Irene's new grad. You used to come down to my ER at four in the morning for the good coffee. It took Maria a second. Asha Shah had run nights in the Greeley ER for most of the years Maria was learning where it was. She's been watching for you since nine. Go on in. Then she was in her car and gone.

Irene was at the kitchen table with two mugs already poured. She was smaller than Maria remembered. Her eyes weren't. Santos. Four years. I'm sorry. I left your party early, and then I never called. You're here now. Sit down before it gets cold.

So Maria sat, and because it was easier, she started with work. Tributary. Forty good pages and a failover nobody had ever run. A first real test in January, three months after three hospitals would depend on it. Irene listened without interrupting, eyes on Maria's face. Then she got up, went to the hall closet, and came back with a binder gone soft at the corners. GREELEY ICU DOWNTIME, in marker, and under it, 2007.

My second year, I lost a man because the paper forms were in a locked closet and nobody had the key, she said, and that was all she ever said about it. So after the long one in 2007, I wrote this, and we practiced it every quarter whether anybody liked it or not. You run the mock code before anybody codes.
Maria turned the pages. Paper order sheets. A census grid. A call tree full of numbers that had been dead for a decade. Near the back, on different paper, was a page Irene had added later.
Transfers by fax. Count the pages against the cover sheet. If the cover sheet is missing, or the count is wrong, call the sending hospital before the first dose. No exceptions on nights. I.K.
There was no date on it. It didn't need one. You wrote this after me. Irene didn't pretend not to understand. After us.

In fourteen years on the same unit, neither of them had ever said it out loud. Now it came out in pieces, the way report comes out at shift change, each of them filling in what the other skipped. A man sent from a small hospital in Wyoming, straight up to the ICU in the middle of the night, no stop in the ER. The fax machine at the charge desk. Irene pulling the sheet off the machine and putting it in Maria's hand. Here's his list. One page. It ended near the bottom, and it looked finished.

There was a page two. There was a page two. The anticoagulant he took at home had been on it. Maria had been minutes from starting him on another one. She'd caught it, and in eighteen years she'd never found a better word for how than luck. She'd hated the word the whole time.

I handed it to you, Irene said. I was charge. Never looked for a cover sheet. Gave a new grad a sick man and half a list and went back to my desk. She turned her mug a quarter turn on the table. I still think about that page every time I hear a fax machine. Which isn't often anymore, thank God. All these years I figured you were being nice to me. I never mentioned it because it was mine. It was mine, Irene. Irene put her hand flat on the binder. Then it's ours. And we've each been hauling it around alone for eighteen years, like a pair of mules. Couple of geniuses. Maria laughed, wet and too loud, and Irene pushed the tissues at her without looking, the same way she used to toss a warm blanket across the charge desk at 4 AM.

Theo tells me your girl's coming to Greeley for nursing school. August. She wants the real story. I keep saying not tonight. Then quit saying it. Tell her the whole thing. Not the version for committees. The part about luck, too. She slid the binder across the table. Take it. It's out of date. The idea isn't. Then she was a charge nurse again. Now. Your vendor. When's the mock code?

Maria tells her what she'll ask for on Monday. Before go-live, Tributary fails its platform over to its second region for real, on a Saturday, with Nate's team watching and a clock running against Cascade's recovery targets. At the same hour, the Wyoming units run their downtime procedures on paper, start to finish. Irene hears the whole plan out, and then she nods once. That's a mock code. She pours them both more coffee. It's gone cold. Neither of them gets up to warm it.

Tuesday, May 18, at 7:30, Nate came to Ochoa's office with Maria and a one-page draft. One row for every system in One Chart: back within four hours, lose no more than one hour. He'd brought it from his last hospital.
Glenn's analyst had already priced the other way, the one Aisha had asked for in an email: every system on hot standby, back in minutes, nothing lost. $3.1 million over five years.
Ochoa read both and slid them across the table to Maria. Neither one of these came from a nurse.

Three weeks of short interviews. Maria and Nate ask each owner the same questions. What happens to patients and the operation at fifteen minutes down? At an hour? At a day? The CNOs answer for the chart, the lab director for results, the revenue cycle director for billing, the analytics director for the warehouse. Gail answers for Rawlins without being asked. The targets come back different for every system, and each owner signs their own row on May 28. Hot standby goes only to the chart, where an hour matters. The cost drops to $1.4 million. Glenn checks the math and sends back one word. Approved.
Thursday, June 3, the owners' targets were taped to Maria's wall, one page, every row signed.

One Chart recovery targets. Corvane EHR. Back within one hour. Lose no more than fifteen minutes.. Tributary transfer feeds. Back within four hours. Lose nothing. Every message delivered or replayed.. Lab system. Back within four hours. Lose no more than fifteen minutes.. Billing. Back within twenty-four hours. Lose no more than one hour.. Patient portal. Back within twenty-four hours. Lose no more than four hours.. Data warehouse. Back within seventy-two hours. Lose no more than twenty-four hours.

Nate stood in front of it with a network map of Wyoming. Rawlins reached Cascade over one circuit from one carrier, buried along the interstate. When a road crew cut it in February, Rawlins lost its lab feeds and the exchange for eleven hours, and MedaLink, on a server in the hospital's basement, kept running. After October, Rawlins' chart would live in Fort Collins, three hours away by road.

The data center can be perfect, Nate said. If the line's cut, Rawlins can't reach it. The carrier's contract says four hours to repair. In February it took eleven. Gail was on the speaker from Rawlins. Eleven hours with a chart I can't open is a long night.

Nate finds a second carrier with fiber along the rail line, a different trench in a different right of way, and the routers switch between the two on their own. On every Rawlins unit, a downtime computer on battery, with its own printer, keeps a read-only copy of the census, active medications, allergies, and the last day of results, refreshed every fifteen minutes. Gail asks who tests it. Nate says the units do, every quarter, by pulling the plug. On purpose? That's the only test that counts.

Tuesday, June 8, Kiran brought Maria a mapping problem with three answers. MedaLink at Laramie stamped admit time when a bed was assigned. Cheyenne stamped it when the patient reached the unit. Corvane stamped it when the doctor signed the admit order. Three different moments, sometimes six hours apart, all called admit time.

Every report that used it would jump at go-live: length of stay, ED boarding, the transfer numbers in Glenn's business case. Aisha wanted Corvane's meaning. Gail wanted Cheyenne's, because that was when her nurses took over. Kiran had a fourth idea, and a spreadsheet.

The data governance council meets on the 17th. Patient flow data belongs to the CNOs, and they settle it in one meeting with Aisha in the room. Admit time is when the admit order is signed. Arrival on the unit gets its own field, so Gail keeps her hour. The HIM director, the steward, writes both into the data dictionary with an owner, a definition, and the date it changed. Converted records keep their old meaning in a note, and every trend report gets a marked line at October. Kiran reads the entry and lets out a breath. So it isn't mine to decide. Nope. It's yours to build.

Tuesday, June 15, Corvane's conversion lead brought the first test load of the master patient index. Of 186,000 Wyoming patients, 141,000 matched someone already in Corvane with near certainty. Another 6,200 were possible matches: the same name and birthday at a different address, or the same everything with one digit off.
Reviewing 6,200 by hand takes two months, he said. We can lower the threshold and merge them automatically. Most of them are the same person.
Most. Maria thought about a chart split in two, half a patient's history in a record nobody would think to open. It was a missing page with a different name.

The HIM director, the index's steward, puts three trained reviewers on it, one paid for by Corvane under the statement of work. They finish in seven weeks. Most pairs are the same person, as promised. Forty-one aren't: twins, a father and son in Rawlins with the same name at the same ranch address, two women in Laramie with the same birthday and the same married name. The lower threshold would have put each pair's medications and allergies in one chart. After the load the duplicate rate is 0.4 percent, and the HIM director sets a target to keep it under one.

Tuesday, June 22, the Clinical Informatics Council met with three new chairs at the table, one for each Wyoming hospital. Kiran's thirty-four Wyoming order sets were on the screen beside Corvane's system sets, the ones the other eight hospitals used.
Walt had marked his up in red. Mine's two clicks shorter than yours, he told the system's chief of surgery, over the speaker from Laramie. I'll trade you.

Kiran had already written it up. His team would own all of them, system and Wyoming, and keep them current. He looked like he hadn't slept, and he probably hadn't. At the break Maria asked him when he'd done it. He shrugged.

When I was a pharmacy tech, I was the one they called at two in the morning, because I knew where everything was, he said. I liked being that guy. I guess I still do. Maria knew exactly what that felt like, which was the problem.

The council takes them one at a time over four meetings. Where Wyoming's set is better, it wins: Walt's discharge set beats the system's by two clicks and becomes everyone's. Every set gets a physician or pharmacist owner, a review date two years out or sooner when the evidence changes, a version number, and a form for requesting changes. Usage reports go to the council every quarter, and sets nobody opens get retired. Kiran builds them. He doesn't own them. Aisha puts the sepsis alert on the same schedule. Everything gets a birthday, she says, and a doctor who has to show up to it.

Tuesday, June 29, Maria went down to the Relay room, where Marcus had a whiteboard covered in boxes and two junior analysts covered in questions. One Chart would bring smart infusion pumps to Laramie and Rawlins. Corvane would send the ordered rate to the pump, and the pump would send back what it gave.
Marcus taught every afternoon now. He pointed her to a chair without stopping. Sit. You're about to learn something too.

The biomed manager from Laramie was on the phone. Her new pumps were in boxes, and Corvane's build team wanted them on the hospital's main network next week, plugged in like everything else, so testing could start.

Marcus runs it as a lesson. His two analysts write the test plan while he watches: every drug in the library, every concentration, the ordered rate going out and the given volume coming back. Pharmacy owns the drug library and signs it. Biomed puts the pumps on their own segment of the network, where Nate can watch them. Nursing picks twenty real scenarios from the Laramie floor. In the first test Corvane sends a heparin rate in milliliters an hour, the pump reads it as units an hour, and one of the analysts catches it before Marcus does. He doesn't say anything. He writes her name on the whiteboard, under his.

Wednesday, July 7, Gail called about the portal. Fourteen percent of Rawlins patients had signed up for MedaLink's, and most of them used it to pay bills. Corvane's portal did more: results, medication lists, messages to the care team, video visits. It also let patients connect apps of their own choosing to their record through a FHIR interface, the kind federal rules now expect.
Half my patients lose signal at the cattle guard, Gail said. The other half have a grandkid who sets up their phone at Christmas. Don't tell me about apps.

Two years of MedaLink results and medication lists convert into Corvane, so the portal has something in it on day one. Before discharge, a nurse or a unit clerk signs the patient up on the patient's own phone, or on a caregiver's, with proxy access the patient approves. Patients who'd rather use an app can connect one. Patients with no signal can get results by phone. Gail picks the measures herself: sign-ups, results viewed, and how many heart failure patients message about their weight before they come back through her ED. Fine. Christmas comes early.

Tuesday, July 13, Aisha forwarded a pitch with a heart in the subject line. Meadowlark, a startup in Boulder, made a patch that heart failure patients wore at home. It sent heart rhythm, breathing, and movement to the cloud, and an AI model scored each patient's risk of coming back to the hospital. The company offered a free year for a hundred patients.
Wyoming readmits heart failure at almost twice our rate, Aisha said. This is exactly what we should be doing. Let's start at Rawlins in September.

The intake group meets the next week: Aisha, a heart failure nurse from Cheyenne, Nate, Joan, Marcus, and Glenn's analyst. The answers go on a single sheet. The patch is cleared by the FDA as a monitor. The risk score isn't cleared for anything yet, and its study was at two city hospitals. Its data would arrive as a PDF, not through FHIR. Nobody at Cascade watches alerts at night. After the free year, it's $400 a patient a month. They plan a pilot of forty patients for February, after go-live, with a nurse watching alerts on days, a FHIR feed, a matched baseline, and a rule for stopping early. You're slower than I want. And if it works, we'll know why.

Friday, July 16, Corvane's cutover plan listed the applications that would move with the three hospitals. There were nineteen, all clinical. Marcus had his own list, built from every interface that touched MedaLink. It had sixty-three.

Row 47 was Lumen, the discharge forecasting tool that read every admission and discharge. If its MedaLink feed went quiet in October, Lumen would forecast three empty hospitals. Most of the rows after it belonged to departments nobody had asked: a claims scrubber, a staffing system, the dietary feed, a cancer registry, the data warehouse.

By the next Friday, Maria and Marcus had put a family and an owner beside every row. Clinical, twenty-six. Administrative, eleven. Financial, fourteen. Consumer, two. Business intelligence, ten, Lumen among them. Each owner would pick a fate: move it, replace it with Corvane, retire it, or reconnect it through Tributary.

The owners found the rest. The staffing system's vendor would end support next spring, in a letter that had gone to a manager who left in 2025. The claims scrubber's vendor was dropping its on-site version for a cloud one. And the state cancer registry would take only a newer version of the reporting standard after next year. The feed Marcus built for it in 2014 didn't speak that version. Nobody at Cascade had seen any of it.

I built that feed, Marcus said. Nobody told me either. Maria thought about her first morning in the chair, MedaLink's letter, twenty months of notice that had felt like none. That's three more MedaLinks, she said. Small ones. How many are coming that we haven't found?

Maria writes it up, and the design group adopts it before the month is out. Each kind of change gets an owner. Joan watches laws and regulations. Nate watches infrastructure and security. Marcus watches interface standards. Aisha and the chief nursing officers watch clinical practice. Pam Castillo in procurement tracks every vendor's roadmap, and every row of Marcus's list gets a column for its support end date. Whatever they find goes into the same technology intake as Meadowlark, and the design group reads the log on the first Tuesday of every month. The staffing system and the registry feed go into the design with dates beside them. Marcus reads it to the bottom and taps the registry row. So the next letter comes to me. To you, and to the log. Not to somebody who left in 2025.
Tuesday, July 20, at 7:30, Ochoa had the capital plan open. Glenn wants five years of what One Chart will need, he said. Bandwidth, storage, licenses, people. Kiran sent me this.
Five years, he said. He wrote 2032 at the top of his legal pad and looked at it longer than the number needed. Build it for whoever's reading it then.

Kiran's sheet took last year's numbers and added ten percent a year to every line. It was neat, and it had cost him a weekend. Maria thought about the summer. A second circuit to Rawlins. Patients' apps reading the chart. A patch that might send heart rhythms from a hundred ranches. None of it was in last year's numbers.

Maria and Kiran rebuild it Wednesday and Thursday, and he leaves at five both nights. Every line starts with what drives it. Bandwidth: Rawlins' chart in Fort Collins, video visits, patient apps, and a possible patch program, each with its own estimate. Storage: imaging growth and seven years of converted records. Messages through Tributary: transfers, the exchange, and apps. People: two analysts who can read FHIR, which Marcus is already building. Each line names the plan it serves and gets redone every year. Ochoa reads every line. First forecast I've seen that tells me why.

Tuesday, July 27, Gail drove down from Rawlins for the design sign-off and stayed after. She'd been thinking about nights. Rawlins had one doctor in the ED after seven and no critical care nurse at all, so its sickest patients rode three hours to Greeley.
The ones who can't wait three hours are the ones I worry about, she said. Greeley has ICU nurses awake all night. I want them watching my two sickest beds.
Maria knew who'd be awake. Bev Hart, at the charge desk where Irene used to sit, where the fax machine used to be.

Bev comes to the second meeting. Kid, I'm too old for a camera. Then she asks who calls whom, and when, and who can order what, which is how Maria knows she's in. The design is short. Greeley ICU nurses watch two Rawlins beds by video and monitor feed from seven at night to seven in the morning, with the same chart open. The Rawlins nurse stays the patient's nurse. Escalation goes to the Rawlins doctor first, then a Greeley intensivist. Joan and legal check licensing across the state line, and consent. The measures are set before the first night: transfers avoided, time to rescue, and a survey of both units' nurses. It starts in February, after go-live. Bev reads the page. Irene would've liked this. She will. I'm telling her Saturday.

Friday, July 30, Ochoa signed the One Chart design at the round table in his office, with Glenn's initials already on the budget page. A hundred and forty pages: recovery targets with an owner's name on every row, a plan for the road to Rawlins, one meaning for admit time, a patient index, sixty-three applications with somebody's name beside each one.
Nate signed the security pages last, after reading the recovery section one more time. Irene's binder sat on the shelf behind Maria's desk, the one place in the building nobody would try to file it.

It had been three months of asking who owns it. Who owns the minutes, who owns a word, who owns a chart that might be two people, who owns an order set after Kiran stops building it. The answer was almost never IT, and it was almost never her. It was the people who'd carry the consequence. Her job had been to find them and get their names on the page.

Sunday, August 1, Lucia found the binder. Maria had brought it home for the weekend to copy the transfer page, and left it on the kitchen table. Lucia read the cover, then the transfer page, then the cover again.
Count the pages, she read out loud. Is this the story? It's how the story ends. Who wrote it? Irene. After. Lucia was quiet for a second. So Irene knows it, and I don't. Irene was there.

You said when you could tell it all the way through. Maria looked at the page, at the initials at the bottom. After go-live, she said. October. All of it, start to finish. The luck too. Lucia looked up. That's a date. That's a date. Lucia closed the binder slowly, with both hands, the way you'd close something in a museum.

Monday, August 2, the first integrated test cycle ran on everything Corvane and Tributary had built since June. At 5:48 PM Kiran's message came in. A hundred and twenty scripts run. Eighty-nine passed. Thirty-one failed, most of them transfers. He was staying to sort them.
Maria wrote back. Go home. We'll sort them at seven. Then she opened the list.
The first failure on it was a test patient from Rawlins with twenty-three active medications, transferred to Greeley. Twenty had arrived. Nothing on the screen said there were more.
